implementation_notes: Go's goroutines are stackful asymmetric coroutines and the language is built around them: a goroutine has its own growable stack (starting at 2 KB and relocated when it runs out), suspends by saving its register set, and resumes wherever the scheduler chooses - so any ordinary function can block at any depth with no async keyword and no split between async and sync functions. This is exactly the 'function colouring' problem Go's design avoids. The cost is a goroutine per concurrent task (cheap: a few KB), the scheduler's fairness policy, and the requirement that goroutines communicate rather than share - because shared mutable state plus migration is where the races come from. Runtime.Gosched() yields voluntarily and is required in a spin loop, since Go's cooperative preemption cannot preempt a goroutine that never reaches a blocking call.
idiom_name: goroutine (stackful, growable 2 KB stack) plus channels for communication; runtime.Gosched in spin loops
pitfalls: A goroutine blocked on a channel is not 'suspended in a coroutine' - it is parked and costs a descriptor; millions of them cost memory but far less than threads.
A spin loop with no runtime.Gosched starves the whole runtime: Go cannot preempt a goroutine that never reaches a blocking call.
Communicate with channels, not shared memory - a goroutine can migrate to another P between suspension points, so shared state needs explicit synchronisation (which is exactly the channels pattern).
Leaked goroutines: a goroutine blocked on a send nobody receives, or a receive nobody sends to or closes, lives forever. Always pair a blocking operation with ctx.Done().
A goroutine per request with no limit is still a scalability problem if each holds a connection or a downstream token.
